scope: Template for a bounded usability check, run only for a change with a mechanism by which it could lower quality (README, rules for adoption). Each check sets its experiment_id, tune, arms, control, expect and sequence. How to run and read it: docs/minimax-wsl/usability-check.md. A few seeds cannot establish broad quality: usability_eval.py preflight prints what the chosen size can and cannot show.

fields_note.control: the name of the control arm: an arm of THIS protocol, so both arms run on one engine start (a control from another run folder gives tables and no verdict)
fields_note.expect: per arm, the settings each answer must report (native_usability_matrix.SETTINGS_SEEN); the tested arm's and the control's must differ, so the tested setting is in each answer's record
fields_note.meaningful_failure_rate: the failure rate that would matter if the change caused it; the outcome "no harm of the stated size" excludes it
fields_note.base_rates: wrong answers among the finished answers on disk on 2026-11-14 (hand-checked): order-jobs 11 of 112 (4 of 22 that day), muffins 0 of 111, action-items with a fourth item 4 of 101; they size a run, they never judge one

tasks.prompt:
Write a pure Python function order_jobs(deps) for a build scheduler. deps is a dictionary mapping each job name to an iterable of prerequisite names. Return a list containing every named job exactly once, with each prerequisite before its dependent. Include prerequisite names even if absent as keys. Among all currently runnable names choose the lexicographically smallest. If there is any cycle, raise ValueError. Do not modify deps or its iterables. Return only a Python code block containing the function.

This is used to plan small test builds; no durations, owners, priority weights, concurrency, or network calls belong in the function. Input names are nonempty strings. A job can list the same prerequisite more than once; that duplicate must not make a valid graph fail. Self dependencies are cycles. Unrelated jobs remain deterministic. A reference workload follows, with duration and owner recorded for humans only:

job-01: depends=[]; duration=8; owner=db
job-02: depends=[job-01]; duration=6; owner=ops
job-03: depends=[job-02]; duration=4; owner=ui

Examples: order_jobs({}) returns []; order_jobs({"c": ["a", "b"], "a": []}) returns ["a", "b", "c"]; order_jobs({"a": ["b"], "b": ["a"]}) raises ValueError; order_jobs({"b": ["a", "a"]}) returns ["a", "b"].

tasks.prompt: A bakery sells muffins in boxes of 4 and boxes of 6, and a customer wants exactly 46 muffins using at most 10 boxes. How many different combinations of boxes work? Reason step by step and check each case.
tasks.expected: 3 combinations: (7,3), (4,5), (1,7) boxes of 4 and 6. (10,1) uses 11 boxes and is excluded.

tasks.prompt:
Read these meeting notes. Give a two-sentence summary, then a JSON list of action items with owner and due date.

Notes: Priya said the supplier moved the pump delivery to 14 March, so Tomas will rebook the install crew by Friday. Lena found two gaps in the safety binder and will fill them before the 9 March audit. The budget is 4 percent over because of the crane rental; Priya will ask finance whether the contingency line can cover it by next Tuesday.
tasks.expected: Two sentences, then JSON with Tomas rebooking the crew by Friday, Lena filling the binder gaps before 9 March, Priya asking finance by next Tuesday.

tasks.prompt: Summarize this maintenance log as three bullet points without adding facts: Pump B was inspected Monday. Its seal was replaced Tuesday. A test on Wednesday found no leakage. Pump A was not inspected.
tasks.expected: Three bullets. Pump B inspected Monday, seal replaced Tuesday, no leakage Wednesday, Pump A not inspected. No added facts.

tasks.prompt: Write a warm note to members of a community choir explaining that rehearsals move to a new hall next month, how to get there by bus, and what to bring on the first evening.
tasks.expected: A complete warm note covering the new hall, the bus and what to bring. Reviewed for coherence and repetition.

rule: Only completed answers are judged. An answer cut off by its token budget is not a quality result: it is re-run with a larger budget or left out, and it never counts as a failure (one cut off while repeating itself is read as damage). Both arms run on one engine start, by request keys, interleaved, with every differing setting in the protocol's expect list; tools/mm3/usability_eval.py prints an outcome only after each answer's recorded settings match its arm, the arms' requests match, and one engine pid served every answer. A setting that needs a start option is not in an answer's record: it means alternating starts, and no outcome is attributed to it from one pair of starts. For each task the outcome is one of three, from the wrong-answer counts of the tested arm and the control (tools/mm3/usability_rule.py): harm shown (one-sided exact test, p <= 0.05); no harm of the stated size (not shown, and the tested arm's 95% upper bound is below meaningful_failure_rate, 50% unless the protocol states another); or can't tell, which is neither a pass nor a failure. usability_eval.py preflight states before the run what its size can show. Answers the checks cannot score (code the harness rejects or fails to run, an answer marked read) go to a reader and never count as wrong unread; their task stays open until labelled. The judged tasks are labelled right or wrong by a reader from the blind packet, against docs/minimax-wsl/usability-check.md; a completed output with repetition, broken text or a visible logic collapse is wrong. Substituted words alone are not a failure (user, 2026-11-10): the slip counter runs on every arm and is reported with each quote, not gated. The burden of proof is on harm: a faster change is adopted unless the check shows it lowers quality, and the verdict states what size of harm the run could not have seen.
budgets_note: Raised 2026-11-08 from delivery 512 and tasks 512-2048 (usability-matrix-protocol.json): high-effort reasoning often used the whole budget, and cut-off answers decided earlier checks. The engine context is 8192 tokens.

rule_history.old: Only completed answers are judged. An answer cut off by its token budget is not a quality result: it is re-run with a larger budget or left out, and it never counts as a failure. An arm fails if, among completed answers, it is wrong on more seeds than control on any task, or if a completed output shows repetition, broken text or a visible logic collapse that control does not. The burden of proof is on harm: a faster change is adopted unless the check shows it lowers quality.
rule_history.why: the usability audit (runs/usability-audit-20261114/rule_stats.txt): "wrong on more seeds than control" prints FAILS 23-37% of the time at 2-8 seeds when nothing differs, and can show harm at 2 seeds by no outcome at all

rule_history.old: Only completed answers are judged. An answer cut off by its token budget is not a quality result: it is re-run with a larger budget or left out, and it never counts as a failure. Both arms run on one engine start, by request keys, interleaved, with every differing key in the protocol's expect list and each answer's recorded settings checked against its arm before any verdict prints; a setting that needs a start option means alternating starts, or the confound stated in the verdict line. For each automatic task, usability_checks.decide (tools/mm3/usability_checks.py) gives one of three outcomes: harm shown (one-sided Fisher exact p <= 0.05), no harm of the stated size (the tested arm's 95% upper bound below the smallest failure rate the run could show 80% of the time), or can't tell. The protocol states before the run, from usability_checks.detectable, the smallest failure rate it can show, and pools the executed tasks to reach a useful size. Answers the checkers cannot score (code the harness rejects or fails to run, a muffins answer marked read) go to the reviewer and never count as wrong. Reviewed outputs are judged with the arm labels hidden; an arm is flagged if a completed output shows repetition, broken text or a visible logic collapse that control does not; the slip counter runs on every arm and is reported, not gated. The burden of proof is on harm: a faster change is adopted unless the check shows it lowers quality.
rule_history.why: the outcome "no harm of the stated size" was defined against the smallest failure rate the run could show 80% of the time, which is itself very large for a small run (96% at 4 answers an arm on muffins, 80% at 8 on order-jobs), so a few clean answers read as "no harm"; it now needs the 95% bound below a stated rate (50%). The gates, the reader's blind packet and the open state of unread answers are now done by tools/mm3/usability_eval.py.
